notes.front: What is artificial intelligence (AI)?
notes.back: A broad field of computer science that builds systems able to imitate human intelligence in order to carry out tasks.
notes.explanation: The study guide treats machine learning, generative AI and agentic AI as kinds of AI.
notes.example: Like a very capable trainee who can read, reason and decide, but whose 'mind' is software running on computers.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is machine learning (ML)?
notes.back: Training a piece of software, called a model, to make useful predictions or generate content from data.
notes.explanation: The content can include text, images, audio or video, not only predictions.
notes.example: Like learning to judge ripe fruit by handling thousands of pieces, rather than by memorising a written checklist.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, introduction
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: In basic terms, ML is the process of training a piece of software, called a model, to make useful predictions or generate content (like text, images, audio, or video) from data.

notes.front: What is generative AI (gen AI)?
notes.back: A type of AI that produces new content, such as text, images, audio or synthetic data.
notes.explanation: Its defining feature is output that did not exist before, rather than a label or a number.
notes.example: Like an illustrator who has studied thousands of pictures and can now draw a new one to your brief.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data analytics?
notes.back: The science of examining raw data to draw conclusions, by cleaning, transforming and interpreting it.
notes.explanation: Its purpose, in the study guide, is to uncover insights and support decisions.
notes.example: Like a detective sifting through raw clues, tidying them up and working out what they point to.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is business intelligence (BI)?
notes.back: A combination of strategies, processes, applications, data and technologies for collecting, analysing, presenting and monitoring business information.
notes.explanation: Its main goal, as the study guide puts it, is better business decisions.
notes.example: Like a ship's bridge with every gauge in view: past course, current position and a forecast of where you are heading.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is responsible AI, in the study guide?
notes.back: A governance framework that covers the fairness and accountability of AI systems.
notes.explanation: It is about how AI is governed and used, not about any one product.
notes.example: Like a hospital's ethics code: it sets who answers for decisions and checks that patients are treated fairly.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is explainable AI, in the study guide?
notes.back: A part of responsible AI that focuses on a model's internal logic and on making its outputs interpretable.
notes.explanation: It narrows the wider framework down to one question: can people understand why the model said what it said?
notes.example: Like a maths teacher asking you to show your working, not just write the final answer.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two of the tasks the study guide says AI systems perform?
notes.back: Any two of: learning, reasoning, problem-solving and decision-making.
notes.explanation: The guide gives these as examples of the human-like tasks that define the field.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the study guide place machine learning in relation to AI, and what does ML do with data?
notes.back: ML is a subset of AI; it uses algorithms to analyse data, find patterns and make predictions or decisions.
notes.explanation: Its defining feature is improving from experience rather than being explicitly programmed for each case.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In machine learning, what is a model?
notes.back: A mathematical relationship derived from data that an ML system uses to make predictions.
notes.explanation: The course contrasts this with two wrong ideas: a piece of hardware, or a scaled-down copy of the thing studied.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Check Your Understanding”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A model is a mathematical relationship derived from data that an ML system uses to make predictions

notes.front: What are two common uses of generative AI that the study guide names?
notes.back: Any two of: chatbots, content generation and document synthesis.
notes.explanation: All three produce new content, which is what defines generative AI in the study guide.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What views of business operations does business intelligence aim to provide, according to the study guide?
notes.back: Historical, current and predictive views.
notes.explanation: Looking back, at now and ahead is how BI serves its main goal of better business decisions.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Data analytics involves techniques to {{c1::clean, transform and interpret}} data so that insights can be uncovered.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines data analytics as examining raw data to draw conclusions; these are the steps it names.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: By what does Google's ML course group ML systems into supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement learning and generative AI?
notes.back: By how they learn to make predictions or generate content; a system can fall into more than one.
notes.explanation: The four groups describe learning styles, not industries or products.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Types of ML Systems”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: ML systems fall into one or more of the following categories based on how they learn to make predictions or generate content:

notes.front: What does a supervised learning model learn from?
notes.back: Lots of data that includes the correct answers; it finds the connections in the data that produce those answers.
notes.explanation: It is called supervised because a human gives the system data with the known correct results.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Supervised learning”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: These ML systems are "supervised" in the sense that a human gives the ML system data with the known correct results.

notes.front: In supervised learning, how does a regression model differ from a classification model?
notes.back: Regression predicts a number; classification predicts whether something belongs to a category.
notes.explanation: Spotting spam emails, or photos that contain a cat, are the course's classification examples.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Classification”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Classification models predict the likelihood that something belongs to a category. Unlike regression models, whose output is a number, classification models output a value that states whether or not something belongs to a particular category. For example, classification models are used to predict if an email is spam or if a photo contains a cat.

notes.front: What does an unsupervised learning model try to do, and who defines its categories?
notes.back: It looks for meaningful patterns in a dataset, often by clustering; the categories are not defined by you.
notes.explanation: After clustering you may name the groups yourself, based on your understanding of the data.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Unsupervised learning”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Clustering differs from classification because the categories aren't defined by you. For example, an unsupervised model might cluster a weather dataset based on temperature, revealing segmentations that define the seasons. You might then attempt to name those clusters based on your understanding of the dataset.

notes.front: How does a reinforcement learning model learn?
notes.back: By getting rewards or penalties for actions it performs in an environment, producing a policy for earning the most reward.
notes.explanation: The course's examples are robots learning to walk around a room and AlphaGo learning Go.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Reinforcement learning”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Reinforcement learning models make predictions by getting rewards or penalties based on actions performed within an environment. A reinforcement learning system generates a policy that defines the best strategy for getting the most rewards. Reinforcement learning is used to train robots to perform tasks, like walking around a room, and software programs like AlphaGo to play the game of Go.

notes.front: In Google's ML course, what is generative AI as a class of models?
notes.back: A class of models that creates content from user input, such as images, music, jokes or article summaries.
notes.explanation: Its outputs are not limited to text: images, music and edited photos count too.
notes.source: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, “What is Machine Learning?”, “Generative AI”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Generative AI is a class of models that creates content from user input. For example, generative AI can create unique images, music compositions, and jokes; it can summarize articles, explain how to perform a task, or edit a photo.

notes.front: How are AI and ML related, in Google Cloud's explainer?
notes.back: AI is the umbrella term; ML is one field under it, alongside others such as deep learning, robotics and natural language processing.
notes.explanation: So all ML is AI, but plenty of AI is not ML.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “AI vs. Machine Learning: How Do They Differ?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the goal of AI differ from the goal of ML, in Google Cloud's explainer?
notes.back: AI aims to mimic human intelligence to do complex tasks; ML aims to do one specific task accurately by learning patterns from data.
notes.explanation: In the explainer's framing, ML is the engine that lets a wider AI system learn and improve over time.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “AI vs. Machine Learning: How Do They Differ?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does data analytics differ from business intelligence, as the study guide defines them?
notes.back: Analytics is the science of drawing conclusions from raw data; BI is the wider set of strategies and tools for better business decisions.
notes.explanation: The study guide calls analytics a science of examining data, while BI spans strategies, processes, apps, data and technologies.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the study guide, how is agentic AI reshaping the way people work?
notes.back: People use AI systems that interact with one another to complete complex, multistep workflows.
notes.explanation: The study guide's examples include workforce productivity, customer support, product innovation, operations and research.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are three areas of work that the exam guide says agentic AI is reshaping?
notes.back: Any three of: workforce productivity, customer support, sales experiences, product innovation, operations and research.
notes.explanation: The exam guide's list is given as examples, so it is not a closed set.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, section 3.1, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings concerns the hardware and systems that AI runs on?
notes.back: Best infrastructure for AI.
notes.explanation: The study guide lists it first of five; it is about the computing foundation, not the models or apps.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings concerns having your data prepared for AI use?
notes.back: An AI-ready data cloud.
notes.explanation: This benefit is about the data platform side of Google Cloud, as distinct from its models and infrastructure.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings concerns Google's own models?
notes.back: Sophisticated first-party (1P) models.
notes.explanation: First-party means built by Google itself, as opposed to third-party or open models.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings gives developers one place to build AI?
notes.back: All-in-one AI developer platforms.
notes.explanation: This benefit is aimed at the people who build AI, rather than those who only use finished apps.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings lets a business use AI without building it first?
notes.back: Prebuilt AI agents and apps.
notes.explanation: Ready-made agents and applications suit teams that want results without developing their own.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which business problem can ML solve when a company's decisions depend on long lists of hand-written rules?
notes.back: Replacing or simplifying rule-based systems.
notes.explanation: ML learns from data instead of being explicitly programmed, which is how the study guide defines it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kinds of data does the study guide say ML can derive business insights from?
notes.back: Large datasets, both structured and unstructured.
notes.explanation: The exam guide stresses both structured and unstructured data here, not only tidy tables.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides replacing rules and finding insights, what third business problem does the study guide say ML helps solve?
notes.back: Scaling business decisions.
notes.explanation: It completes the study guide's list of three business problems ML can help solve.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does data quality matter for ML, according to the study guide?
notes.back: The accuracy of ML predictions depends on large volumes of data, so flawed data leads to flawed predictions.
notes.explanation: The guide counts data as low quality if it has errors, is not aligned to the problem, or is biased.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The study guide evaluates data against {{c1::six}} dimensions of quality: completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy and consistency.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog uses a slightly different list, with freshness and volume; the exam guide lists the same six as the study guide.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which data-quality dimension asks whether the data holds all the information needed for its intended purpose?
notes.back: Completeness.
notes.explanation: The test is the intended purpose: information that purpose needs, but the data lacks, makes it incomplete.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Completeness assesses whether the data contains all of the information that's required for its intended purpose.

notes.front: Which data-quality dimension measures whether the data is distinct, with no duplicates?
notes.back: Uniqueness.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog lists uniqueness among its data-quality dimensions, as the study guide does.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Uniqueness measures whether the data is distinct with no duplicates.

notes.front: Knowledge Catalog calls one data-quality dimension “freshness”. Which study-guide dimension matches it?
notes.back: Timeliness.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog lets you rename dimensions to your organisation's terms, and gives timeliness as an example name for freshness.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: You can use dimension names that reflect your organization's terminology. For example, instead of freshness, you might use timeliness.

notes.front: Which data-quality dimension checks that data conforms to set standards for format or acceptable ranges?
notes.back: Validity.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog's example: where dates must be written year/month/day, a date written 08-12-2019 is invalid.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Validity evaluates whether the data conforms to built-in standards for format, acceptable ranges, or other criteria. For example, if a valid date needs to have the format YYYY/mm/dd, then 08-12-2019 is invalid data.

notes.front: Which data-quality dimension reflects whether the data is actually correct?
notes.back: Accuracy.
notes.explanation: This is separate from validity: a value can be well formed and still wrong.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Accuracy reflects the correctness of the data. Note that data that is valid isn't necessarily accurate.

notes.front: Which data-quality dimension means the same data has the same values across tables and columns?
notes.back: Consistency.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog's example: a product's revenue differs depending on whether it is read from a sales or a usage database.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Consistency refers to having the same values for data across multiple instances, such as tables and columns. Inconsistency in data arises when, for example, the revenue of a product differs when it is read from a sales database or a usage database.

notes.front: Can data be valid but still inaccurate?
notes.back: Yes. Validity is about meeting format or range rules; accuracy is about being correct.
notes.explanation: Knowledge Catalog's example: “brown” is a valid hair colour, but it is inaccurate for someone whose hair is not brown.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Note that data that is valid isn't necessarily accurate. For example, a valid hair color might be brown, but if a person doesn't have brown hair, that is inaccurate data.

notes.front: What do responsible AI and explainable AI both aim to do, according to the study guide?
notes.back: Build trust and reduce risk by making sure AI is used ethically and safely.
notes.explanation: They share this aim even though explainable AI covers a narrower part of the framework.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is explainability a problem for many ML models, according to Google Cloud's documentation?
notes.back: They are often “black boxes”: even their designers cannot explain how or why a model produced a particular result.
notes.explanation: Google's Vertex Explainable AI, deprecated from 16 March 2026, answered this with feature-based and example-based explanations.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Introduction to Vertex Explainable AI”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Machine learning models are often "black boxes"; even their designers cannot explain how or why a model produced a specific inference. Vertex Explainable AI offers Feature-based and Example-based explanations to provide better understanding of model decision making.

notes.front: Which recommended practices does Google Cloud encourage customers to promote when using its generative AI services?
notes.back: Fairness, interpretability, privacy and security practices; customers also remain responsible for following Google Cloud's Acceptable Use Policy.
notes.explanation: The duty to follow the Acceptable Use Policy and related terms stays with the customer, not with Google.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Responsible AI” (Agent Platform), introduction
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: We encourage customers to promote fairness, interpretability, privacy and security recommended practices . Customers also remain responsible for adherence to Google Cloud's Acceptable Use Policy (AUP), Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy, and any other Service Specific Terms

notes.front: What is bias amplification, as a limitation of generative AI models?
notes.back: Models can unintentionally amplify biases already in their training data, reinforcing prejudice and unequal treatment of some groups.
notes.explanation: The bias starts in the training data, but the model's outputs can make it worse.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Responsible AI” (Agent Platform), “Model limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Bias amplification: Generative AI models can inadvertently amplify existing biases in their training data, leading to outputs that can further reinforce societal prejudices and unequal treatment of certain groups.

notes.front: What do generative AI models need in order to reduce the chance of inaccurate or nonsensical outputs (hallucinations)?
notes.back: Context grounded in real-world information and an accurate understanding of your specific data.
notes.explanation: Without grounding, a model may produce outputs that are inaccurate, irrelevant or nonsensical.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Responsible AI” (Agent Platform), “Model limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Generative AI models require context grounded in real-world information, physical properties, and accurate understanding of your specific data in order to reduce the chance of the model producing inaccurate, irrelevant, or nonsensical outputs.

notes.front: What are edge cases, as a limitation of generative AI models?
notes.back: Unusual, rare or exceptional situations that are poorly represented in the training data.
notes.explanation: They can lead to overconfidence, misreading of context or inappropriate outputs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Responsible AI” (Agent Platform), “Model limitations”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Edge cases refer to unusual, rare, or exceptional situations that are not well-represented in the training data. These cases can lead to limitations in the performance of the model, such as model overconfidence, misinterpretation of context, or inappropriate outputs.

notes.front: What are two of the steps Google Cloud recommends for using generative AI safely and responsibly?
notes.back: Any two of: assess security risks, perform safety testing, configure safety filters, and gather user feedback and monitor content.
notes.explanation: The list runs from assessing risk before launch to monitoring content afterwards.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Responsible AI” (Agent Platform), “Recommended practices”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: We recommend taking the following steps: - Assess your application's security risks. - Perform safety testing appropriate to your use case. - Configure safety filters if required. - Solicit user feedback and monitor content.

notes.front: A travel agency wants software that writes a fresh, personalised holiday itinerary in prose for each customer. Which kind of AI is this?
notes.back: C) Generative AI
notes.choices:
A) Business intelligence dashboards
B) Rule-based automation with no learning
C) Generative AI
D) Clustering historical bookings
notes.choicesExplained: A) Dashboards present and monitor existing data; they don't write new itineraries. B) Fixed rules cannot compose fresh prose for each customer. D) Clustering groups existing records; it does not create content.
notes.explanation: Writing new text on request is producing new content, which is what generative AI does.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A water company wants a system that learns from years of meter readings to predict tomorrow's demand, improving as new readings arrive. Which description fits best?
notes.back: B) Machine learning
notes.choices:
A) Generative AI
B) Machine learning
C) A static report of last year's usage
D) A fixed formula written by an engineer
notes.choicesExplained: A) Generative AI makes new content such as text or images; a demand figure is a prediction. C) A static report describes the past and does not learn. D) A fixed formula does not improve from new data.
notes.explanation: Learning patterns from data and improving with experience, rather than following hand-coded rules, is the study guide's description of ML.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hotel chain wants a company-wide set of processes and tools so that managers everywhere can monitor bookings over time, see current occupancy and view forecasts. Which term fits best?
notes.back: D) Business intelligence
notes.choices:
A) Generative AI
B) Explainable AI
C) A one-off data-cleaning exercise
D) Business intelligence
notes.choicesExplained: A) Generative AI creates new content, not monitoring views. B) Explainable AI is about understanding model outputs. C) Cleaning data is one step of data analytics, not an organisation-wide practice for monitoring.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes BI as strategies, processes, apps and technologies giving historical, current and predictive views of operations.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online retailer deploys AI agents that, on their own, check an order, arrange a courier collection and issue a refund when a customer reports a damaged item. Which area of work from the exam guide does this reshape most directly?
notes.back: B) Customer support
notes.choices:
A) Research
B) Customer support
C) Product innovation
D) Sales experiences
notes.choicesExplained: A) Nothing here investigates or discovers new knowledge. C) The retailer isn't designing new products. D) The customer has already bought; this is after-sales service, not selling.
notes.explanation: The agents carry a multistep workflow through for a customer's problem, which is customer support.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, section 3.1, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A small insurer with no data-science team wants to start using AI within weeks, using agents and applications Google has already built. Which key benefit of Google Cloud's AI offerings matters most here?
notes.back: C) Prebuilt AI agents and apps
notes.choices:
A) All-in-one AI developer platforms
B) Best infrastructure for AI
C) Prebuilt AI agents and apps
D) Sophisticated first-party (1P) models
notes.choicesExplained: A) A developer platform helps people who build AI, which this insurer can't do. B) Infrastructure matters to teams running their own AI workloads. D) Models are ingredients; the insurer wants finished agents and apps.
notes.explanation: The insurer wants to use AI that Google has already built, which is exactly this benefit.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bank's fraud checks rely on thousands of hand-written if-then rules that staff struggle to keep up to date. Which business problem that ML solves does this describe?
notes.back: D) Replacing or simplifying rule-based systems
notes.choices:
A) Scaling business decisions
B) Deriving insights from unstructured data
C) Presenting historical dashboards
D) Replacing or simplifying rule-based systems
notes.choicesExplained: A) Volume of decisions is not the complaint; the rules are. B) Nothing here mentions unstructured data such as documents or images. C) Dashboards are business intelligence, not an ML problem.
notes.explanation: The pain here is the rulebook itself, which is the first business problem the study guide lists for ML.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After merging two customer lists, a firm finds many customers appear twice, which inflates its customer count. Which data-quality dimension has failed?
notes.back: C) Uniqueness
notes.choices:
A) Validity
B) Timeliness
C) Uniqueness
D) Completeness
notes.choicesExplained: B) Timeliness concerns how recent the data is. A) Validity concerns format and allowed ranges. D) Completeness concerns missing information, not repeated records.
notes.explanation: Uniqueness is about data being distinct with no duplicates.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Uniqueness measures whether the data is distinct with no duplicates.

notes.front: A form accepts dates typed in any style, so the order table now mixes 2026/03/01 with “1st March”. Which data-quality dimension is at risk?
notes.back: B) Validity
notes.choices:
A) Uniqueness
B) Validity
C) Consistency
D) Timeliness
notes.choicesExplained: A) The problem is not duplicate records. C) Consistency is about the same value matching across tables, not one field's format. D) Timeliness is about how current the data is.
notes.explanation: Validity checks that data conforms to set standards for format and acceptable ranges.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Validity evaluates whether the data conforms to built-in standards for format, acceptable ranges, or other criteria.

notes.front: A customer's new email address appears in the billing table, but the support team's table still shows the old one. Which data-quality dimension is failing?
notes.back: C) Consistency
notes.choices:
A) Completeness
B) Uniqueness
C) Consistency
D) Validity
notes.choicesExplained: A) Nothing is missing; both tables hold an address. B) There are no duplicate rows. D) Both addresses may be well formed; the problem is that they disagree.
notes.explanation: Consistency means the same data has the same values across tables and columns.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Auto data quality overview”, “Dimensions”

notes.evidence: Consistency refers to having the same values for data across multiple instances, such as tables and columns.

notes.front: A lender's model refuses some loan applications, and the regulator asks the lender to show which factors drove each refusal. Which idea addresses this most directly?
notes.back: C) Explainable AI
notes.choices:
A) Business intelligence
B) Generative AI
C) Explainable AI
D) Scaling business decisions
notes.choicesExplained: B) Generative AI creates content; it does not explain a lending model. A) BI reports on business operations, not on why a model decided. D) Scaling decisions is a benefit of ML, not a way of explaining them.
notes.explanation: The regulator is asking about the model's internal logic and how to interpret its outputs, the focus of explainable AI.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council sets up a board that checks its AI systems for unfair outcomes and decides who is accountable when they go wrong. Which idea does this put into practice?
notes.back: B) Responsible AI
notes.choices:
A) Data analytics
B) Responsible AI
C) Explainable AI only
D) Supervised learning
notes.choicesExplained: A) Analytics draws conclusions from data; it is not a governance framework. D) Supervised learning is a way models learn. C) Explainable AI covers interpretability only, a narrower part of what the board does.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines responsible AI as a governance framework for fairness and accountability.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does explainable AI differ from responsible AI?
notes.back: Responsible AI is the wider governance framework for fairness and accountability; explainable AI is a part of it focused on interpreting model outputs.
notes.explanation: One is about how AI is governed overall; the other is about whether its reasoning can be understood.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Innovating with Google Cloud Artificial Intelligence”, p. 6
